(From the judgment and order dated 7-4-2011 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 507, 26 and 27 of 2011) with CPLA Nos. 1948, 2170, 2184 of 2011 with CPLA No. 2206 of 2011. with 
CPLA No. 1947 of 2011. with CPLA No. 2169 of 2011.
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: The delay in filing of the leave petitions is condoned. Though the facts, the status of the writ petitioners, and the judgments are not identical rather distinct, law points involved in these petitions being almost identical, these petitions are disposed of analogously by this Order. Facts relevant for the disposal of these petitions are as under:

CP No. 1247 of 2011

2. This petition arose from the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 8737 of 2008. In the High Court Division 49 persons filed the above writ petition seeking a direction upon the writ respondents who are petitioners herein to issue permanent appointment letters in the respective posts or in the alternative, they sought for transferring their services in the revenue set up. They claimed that they were appointed in different projects under the Local Government Engineering Division (LGED) of the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives. Some of the writ petitioners are Work Assistants, others are Community Organizers, Sub-Assistant Engineers, Drivers, Computer Operators, Account Assistants, Surveyors and Roller Drivers. The LGED issued a circular regarding assimilation of the employees of development budget to the revenue budget and pursuant thereto some of them were assimilated but the writ petitioners were not regularized despite their long years in service to the satisfaction of the authority. A Division Bench of the High Court Division presided over by AHM Shamsuddin Chowdhury, J by the impugned judgment dated 10th May, 2010 observed that the writ petitioners have legitimate expectation to be absorbed in the revenue budget and accordingly made the Rule absolute. The High Court Division however, did not give any direction to regularize the petitions in the revenue set up.

CP No. 1948 of 2011

3. This petition arose from the judgment in Writ Petition No. 3302 of 2010 in which there are 102 petitioners. They claimed as Work Assistant, Account Assistants, Computer Operators, Clerk-cum typists, Surveyors working in different projects under LGED and some of them are working on daily master roll basis. It is stated that the writ respondents regularized some employees of the LGED who worked under different projects but the authority did not absorb the writ petitioners. They can legitimately claim of their absorption since other employees have been absorbed in the revenue set up. They sought for a direction for their absorption in the revenue set up. A Division Bench of the High Court Division presided over by AHM Shamsuddin Chowdhury, J noticed ECNEC decision dated 10th June, 2008 and directed the writ respondents to absorb the writ petitioners in the revenue budget on being satisfied that they are not otherwise disqualified.

CP No. 2170 of 2011

4. This petition arose from the judgment of High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 5367 of 2010, in which, there are 31 petitioners, of them, it is stated, the writ petitioner Nos.1-21 are working as Work Assistants, Nos. 22-25 are working as Office Assistants and Nos. 26-31 are working as Computer-Operators and Typists in different projects of the LGED. The LGED published the advertisements for recruitment of Work Assistants, Computer Operators and Office Assistants against which the writ petitioner and others filed the Petition No. 1152 of 2006 in the High Court Division. The High Court Division stayed the recruitment process and during the pendency of the said Rule, the LGED without following the rules and guidelines absorbed some employees on pick and choose basis in the revenue budget. The High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 3218 and 4455 of 2010 issued similar nature of rules in respect of other employees. Since they have been working in different projects from 5 years to 21 years, they have already crossed the age limit of 30 years for entering into the Government service. A Division Bench of the High Court Division presided by AHM Shamsuddin Chowdhury J উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হইতে রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরিতের পদধারীদের নিয়মিত করন ও জ্যেষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ বিধিমালা. (the Rules of 2005) and the ECNEC's decision dated 10th January, 2008 made the rule absolute directing the writ respondents in the following term to absorb the petitioners in the revenue budget when, however, vacancy occurs upon satisfaction that the latter can satisfy the criteria laid down in clause 4 of the rule contained in the gazette cited above or they can bring themselves within the purview of ECNEC resolution, or that those, whose jobs were previously regularized on pick and chose basis, do not stand on the criteria".

CP No 2184 of 2011

5. This petition arose from the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 4666 of 2010 in which there are 45 petitioners. The writ petitioners stated that they have been working as Work Assistants, Account Assist-ants, Office Assistants and Computer Operators on master role basis. Some Assistant Engineers while serving under different projects filed 100 writ petitions for being absorbed in the revenue budget, the High Court Division made the rule absolute which judgment was affirmed up to this Division. The writ respondents did not absorb the writ petitioners and invite fresh advertisements and instead of regularizing their service of the writ petitioners committed illegality in making advertisements for recruitments which is illegible. The writ petitioners have legitimate expectation for being absorbed in the revenue set up. Same Bench of the High Court Division made the rule absolute on similar terms as in Writ Petition No. 5367 of 2010.

CP No. 2169 of 2011

6. This petition arose out of Writ Petition No. 11152 of 2006. In the above writ petition, 48 writ petitioners who are Computer Operators, Work Assistants, Roller Drivers, MLSS, Surveyor, Office Assistants, Drivers, Typists, Accountants, Account Assistants sought similar relief.

7. Writ petitioners stated that the Superintending Engineer, the respondent No. 3, published two advertisements, one on 3rd November, 2006, and other on 28th October, 2006 inviting applications for appointment to some posts without regularizing the writ petitioners services in the title revenue set up who have been serving for a long time. Some of the employees of LGED have been transferred to the revenue set up but the writ respondents did not regularize the writ petitioners. They made representations for their regularization and every time they were assured, but ultimately no order was passed. A Division Bench of the High Court Division presided over by AHM Shamsuddin Chowdhury, J upon hearing the parties, by the impugned judgment dated 29th March 2011, made the Rule absolute and directed the writ respondents to absorb the writ petitioners in the revenue set up whenever vacancy occurs pointing out "upon satisfaction that the latter can satisfy the criteria laid down in clause 4 of the rule- contained in the gazette cited above or they can bring themselves within the purview of the ECNEC resolution, or that those whose jobs were previously regularized on pick and chose basis do not stand on different posts."

CP No. 1784 of 2011

8. This petition arose out of the judgment dated 7th April, 2011 of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 26 of 2011. The High Court Division heard the above writ petition along with writ Petition Nos. 27 of 2011 and 507 of 2011. In Writ Petition No. 26 of 2011, 33 petitioners who are Assistant Engineers, Estimators, and some of them did not mention their status, claimed that they were appointed in different projects in the LGED and after completion of one project, they were transferred to another project and this way they have been working for a long time. They claimed that they made several correspondences for regularization of their services in the revenue set up but the concerned Ministry without following the rules on pick and choose basis absorbed some employees in the revenue set up. They have been working for about 5-20 years in different projects. They claimed that 2559 posts are lying vacant in the LGED and therefore, there will be no complication if they are regularized in the revenue set up.

9. Another Division Bench of the High Court Division presided over by Md Momtaz Uddin Ahmed, J. following the judgment in Writ Petition No. 3218 of 2010, in which, it was directed upon the writ respondents to consider the cases of the writ petitioners for regularizing in the revenue budget, directed the writ respondents to "regularize the service of the petitioners in revenue head in the Local Government Engineer Department."

CP No. 1781 of 2011

10. This petition arose out of the judgment in Writ. Petition No. 507 of 2011. In the above petition there are 68 writ petitioners who claimed that they are Estimators, Draftsmen, Supervisors and Sub-Assistant Engineers. They also claimed that they were appointed in different projects of the LGED and have been working in different projects and after completion of one project they were transferred to another project. They claimed that as per policy of the Government, the respondents ought to have transferred the services to the revenue set up after their projects were ended but their services were not regularized. They are academically qualified and skilled in their respective fields. They state that the writ respondents regularized 3285 employees of various development projects under similar situation without considering the cases of the writ petitioners and thereby, they have been deprived of legitimate right of absorption, They claimed to be regularized on the principle of legitimate expectation in the revenue set up. As observed above, this petition was disposed of by the same Bench along with Writ Petition No. 26 of 2011.

CP No. 1875 of 2011

11. This petition arose out of the judgment in Writ Petition No. 27 of 2011 which was heard and disposed of along with Writ Petition Nos. 26 of 2011 and 507 of 2011. In this petition there are 62 writ petitioners, of them some are Accountants, Account Assistants, Work Assistants, Office Assistants, Computer Operators and some of others are Surveyors, Laboratory Technicians, Drivers, Roller Drivers and MLSS. They stated that they were appointed in different development projects. They made different correspondences to regularize their services in the revenue budget but the authority without following rules and guidelines absorbed some other employees but discriminated against them in considering their cases. They also stated that some of them have already crossed 30 years of age and therefore, they are not eligible to apply for government jobs in the LGED department. They claimed that there are 2559 vacant posts lying in the LGED and, as such, no complication would arise if the petitioners services are regularized in the revenue set up. They prayed for regularization of their services and the High Court Division accordingly directed the writ respondents to regularize their services in the revenue set up.

CP No. 2206 of 2011

12. This petition arose out of the judgment Writ Petition No. 3293 of 2010 in which there are 109 petitioners. In the writ petition they did not state their status either in the cause titles or in the statement of facts. They simply stated that they were appointed on temporary basis under project in several districts under the master roll program. After completion of the project, they were transferred to another project. They were not regularized in the revenue set up although the Government published notification dated 10th December, 2009 for new recruitment. They made different representations up to the Prime Minister but their prayers were not acceded to. A Division Bench of the High Court Division presided over by Md. Mamtaz Uddin Ahmed, J made the rule absolute in the similar terms as made in Writ Petition No. 507 of 2011 and directed the writ respondents to regularize the services of the writ petitioners against their respective posts.

13. As observed above, the writ petitioners claimed to be absorbed in the revenue set up on the doctrine of legitimate expectation on the ground that in pursuance of the judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 1522 of 2004 along with 99 other petitions which was heard and disposed of by Judgment dated 16 March, 2006 by a Division Bench presided over Md Abdul Matin, J. Some Sub-Assistant Engineers worked in development project of LGED were absorbed in the revenue set up. Those petitions were filed by Sub-Assistant Engineers seeking prohibitory orders not to issue appointment letters of 98 regular Assistant Engineers/ Upazila Engineers in pursuance of the notification issued by the Public Service Commission on 7th February, 2004. They claimed that they were experienced engineers working in the same department for about 5 years but because of the age bar and in the absence of any provision for application by in-service persons, they could not apply for the posts. It was their claim that in selecting the posts in the revenue set up, neither Rule nor Regulation was followed and that the authority adopted pick and choose policy. They claimed regularization on the doctrine, legitimate expectation.

<u>14. The High Court Division did not accept the contention observing "it is true that even legitimate expectation does not by itself give rise to any right in absence of any express promise or representation or by established policy or settled principle but facts remain that the matter of regularization of the existing Assistant Engineers was pending for a long time and the matter was processed by the department within the knowledge of the petitioners and at no point of time prospect of regularization was negative for the higher authorities and therefore, the petitioners had been expecting their regularization and in view of the admitted position the ultimately regularization was done further justifies the cases of the petitioners legitimate expectation of being considered along with the proposed Assistant Engineers who have been proposed to be regularized". The High Court Division further observed that the "the regularization of other 99 persons has a presumption of correctness and respondents do not say that it was done illegally. From the reply to affidavit-in-opposition it appears that the respondents have already kept 98 posts of Assistant Engineers vacant and therefore in fitness of things they should consider the present cases, in the same way as has been done in the cases of 99 Assistant Engineers as in Annexures-F and F-1 to the Writ petition in accordance with law".</u>

15. With these observations the High Court Division disposed of all the rules with a direction upon the LGED to consider the cases of 100 writ petitioners in the same way as has been done in the case of 99 Assistant Engineers. The petitioners filed leave petitions against the said judgment. This Division granted leave to the petitioners but ultimately the appeal was not pressed. Pursuant thereto, those 99 Assistant Engineers were absorbed in the LGED. The facts of those cases are quite distinguishable but the High Court Division relying upon the said judgment allowed huge number of writ petitions and directed the authority to absorb them in the revenue budget.

<u>16. There should not be conflicting opinions of different Benches of the High Court Division sitting on coordinate jurisdiction. When there will be different opinions on a particular point, it will be difficult for the executive to follow the directions. Whenever, a Division Bench of the High Court Division is called upon to decide question of law, it becomes its duty to ascertain whether any pronouncement of the High Court Division exists on the point and the best procedure is to follow the said opinion. If it does not accept the decision as correct, it may refer the matter to a Full Bench after formulating the point on which it differs on the point of law. If the facts are distinguishable then it can decide the question of law on the facts of the given case. In these cases we noticed that though their attention was drawn to the earlier pronouncement, each Bench expressed its own opinion ignoring earlier opinions.</u>

17. One Division Bench which decided the first set of cases was of the view that the legitimate expectation does not give rise to any right to an employee in the absence of promise or representation on the part of LGED and that since LGED has kept 98 posts of Assistant Engineers vacant, the LGED should have considered the cases of writ petitioners in the said post as has been done in respect of 99 of posts. In the present cases, one Division Bench directed LGED to absorb writ petitioners in the revenue set up on the doctrine of legitimate expectation and another Division Bench made two conflicting opinions. One opinion is that the writ petitioners have legitimate expectation, and there is violation of Article 29 of the Constitution since some other employees have been absorbed in the revenue set up. In another set of judgment, the same Bench considered the Ministry of Finance's Circular dated 3rd October, 2000 but it did not consider the ECNEC's decision dated 10th January, 2008, which was considered in earlier judgments by the same Bench and ultimately directed that the writ petitioners should be absorbed in the revenue set up. In another set of judgments, the same Division Bench considered the Rules, 2005, the ECNEC's decision dated 10th January, 2008 and thereupon directed the writ respondent to absorb the writ petitioners in the revenue set up upon satisfaction that the writ respondents can satisfy the criteria laid down in rule 4 of the Rules of 2005 and ECNEC's resolution.

18. Learned Attorney-General took us to the judgment and submitted that the High Court Division committed a fundamental error in making the rules absolute on the doctrine of legitimate expectation which doctrine has no manner of application against the Government or its departments in the absence of any promise or assurance and that's too, in the absence of foundation and proper pleadings. Learned Attorney-General contends that since there are conflicting opinions by three Benches of the High Court Division, ends of justice demands that the judgments are required to be examined by this Division.

19. The doctrine off legitimate expectation is a concept which is akin to that a promissory estoppels and this concept has been developed in the European Community Law. According to the doctrine, where a person is the victim of an unfavourable decision taken by a public authority, this may amount to an infringement of that person's legitimate expectation, where, for example, the decision contradicts an earlier promise or course of conduct on the part of the public authority concerned. Therefore, this doctrine is circumscribed by certain limitations and exceptions. The first and foremost consideration is that there must be a foundation in the petition claiming legitimate expectation and secondly, there must be a promise or a representation on the part of the public authority on the claim of the persons aggrieved by the decision. In this connection it will be profitable if I reiterate an observation of the Supreme Court of India in case of National Buildings Construction Corporations vs Raghunathan, AIR 1998 SC 2779, as under:—

"Incidentally, in this case what question of 'Legitimate Expectation' and not raised in the petition and foundation was laid in the pleadings for such a plea being advanced before the Court. Strangely, the High Court allowed this plea at the stage of argument and allowed the petitions only on the ground of 'Legitimate Expectation' without least realizing that there was hardly any legitimacy in the claim of the respondents. In the absence of pleading and the affidavit of the respondents and support thereof, the whole exercise done by the High Court cannot but be termed to be speculative."

20. In Council of Civil Service Union vs Ministry for the Civil Service, (1984) 3 All ER 935, the House of Lords observed on the principle as under:

"An aggrieved person was entitled to invoke judicial review if he showed that a decision of a public authority affected him by depriving him of some benefit or advantage which in the past he had been permitted to enjoy and which he could legitimately expect to be permitted to continue to enjoy either until he was given reasons for its withdrawal and the opportunity to comment on those reasons or because he had received an assurance that it would not be withdrawn before he had been given the opportunity of making representations against the withdrawal. The appellants legitimate expectation arising from the existence of a regular practice or consultation which the appellants could reasonably expect to continue gave rise to an implied limitation on the Minister's exercise of the power contained in Art. 4 of the 1995 order, namely an obligation to act fairly by consulting the GCHQ staff before withdrawing the benefit of Trade Union membership."

21. Supreme Court of India in Food Corporation of India vs Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries Ltd. (1993) 1 SCC 71, observed:

"The mere reasonable or legitimate expectation of a citizen, in such a situation, may not by itself by a distinct enforceable right, but failure to consider and give due weight to it may render the decision arbitrary, and this is how the requirement of due consideration of a legitimate expectation forms part of the principle of non-arbitrariness, a necessary concomitant of the rule of law. Every legitimate expectation is a relevant factor requiring due consideration in a fair decision-making process. Whether the expectation of the claimant is reasonable or legitimate in the context is a question of fact in each case. Whenever the question arises, it is to be determined not according to the claimant's perception but in larger public interest wherein other more important considerations may outweigh what would otherwise have been the legitimate expectation of the claimant. A bona fide decision of the public authority reached in this manner would satisfy the requirement of non-arbitrariness and withstand judicial scrutiny. The doctrine of legitimate expectation gets assimilated in the rule of law and operates in our legal system in this manner and to this extent."

22. Similar views were taken by this Division in Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation vs Nasir Ahmed Chowdhury, 7 MLR (AD) 265 = 7 BLC (AD) 144. In this case this Division approved the views taken in the case of Hindustan Development Corporation. It is observed that the concept of legitimate expectation can have no role to play and the Court must not usurp discretion of the public authority which is empowered to take the decisions under law and the Court is expected to apply an objective standard which leaves to the deciding authority the full range of choice which the legislature is presumed to have intended. The Court will not interfere on the ground of procedural fairness to a person whose interest based on legitimate expectation might be affected.

<u>23. The writ petitioners have failed to make out a case of their being absorbed in the revenue set up on the doctrine of legitimate expectation. In some petitions they stated that they made representations which did not fructify a right to be claimed on the doctrine. There is nothing to assume that the LGED assured them to regularize their services in the revenue set up. Nor did the LGED withdraw the benefits which they enjoyed earlier. Further, a claim on the principle will not be an enforceable right, at best, they can claim a fair decision whenever a post is lying vacant in the revenue set up and under such circumstances, the High Court Division may direct LGED to consider their cases. The doctrine of legitimate expectation, apart from the above, cannot be claimed by a temporary or casual worker who has been employed on contractual basis. It is not their case that at the time of their appointments they were assured that they would be regularized in due course in the revenue set up. The High Court Division failed to notice that the absorption of some officers and employees were made in pursuance of the directions given by the High Court Division on different context. On perusal of the appointment letters on some writ petitioners, I have noticed that the appointments were made on temporary basis on attaching conditions that they could be removed without issuing any show cause notice after the completion of the projects. In some appointment letters, it was mentioned that if their services are not satisfactory to the authority, they may be removed without any show cause notice. In the premise, the High Court Division wrongly applied the said doctrine.</u>

24. Learned Attorney-General submitted that admittedly some of the writ petitioners were appointed on master roll basis, who cannot claim as of right to be appointed on regular basis in the revenue set up particularly when the LGED has framed rules for recruitment. In this connection the learned Attorney-General has drawn our attention to “স্থানীয় সরকার প্রকৈাশল অধিদপ্তর (কর্মকর্তা/কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা, ২০০৯” and submits that in presence of the rule for recruitment, none of the writ petitioners can claim as of right to be absorbed, and therefore, the High Court Division erred in law in directing the writ respondents to absorb the writ petitioners in the revenue set up. Learned Attorney-General has also referred the case Secretary, State of Karnataka vs Umadevi (2006) 4 SCC 1 in support of his contention.

<u>25. True, some of the writ petitioners were appointed on master roll basis and some of them were appointed on monthly pay basis. The writ petitioners out of which CP Nos. 1984 of 2011, 2084 of 2011 and 2206 of 2011 arose were admittedly appointed on master roll basis. They however, claimed that they are qualified to be absorbed in the revenue budget and that some of them made representations for their absorption. Though in some petitions the writ petitioners stated that 2559 posts are lying vacant but they did not specifically mention the number of posts lying vacant against different categories of posts. So the statements as regards their claim of absorption against vacant posts are vague and indefinite. Learned Attorney-General has drawn our attention to some documents which have been accompanied with the additional paper book filed on 6th February, 2012 in CP No. 1781, 1784 and 1785 of 2011 and tries to convince us that there is no vacant post in the LGED. This being a disputed question we are not inclined to enter into this disputed fact at this stage.</u>

26. In Umadevi (supra) referred above, similar nature of directions were given by different High Courts of India and, as a result, the Supreme Court noticed that the suitable candidates were being deprived of public employments and that for public appointments certain laws were made by the Central Government and Provincial Governments including the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, providing provisions for giving employment to at least one member of a family for 100 days a year on paying wages. The Central Government and State Governments have resorted to irregular appointments even by-passing Public Service Commissions, keeping out those who are qualified to apply for the posts through back door, sometimes on daily basis. They then approach Courts seeking directions to make them permanent in their posts and to prevent regular recruitments. The High Courts directed as per prayers made ignoring the legal aspects. The Constitutional Bench noticed that the Supreme Court also issued directions which were inconsistent with the constitutional scheme of public employment, presumably on the basis of equitable considerations. In the context of the matter, the Supreme Court posed a question as to equity for whom? It then answered, equity for the handful of people who have approached the Court with a claim; or equity for the teeming millions seeking employment and seeking a fair opportunity for competing for employment? In that case two sets of appeals, in one set of appeal some persons temporarily engaged on daily wages worked for more than 10 years claimed permanent employment by filing a writ petition in the Karnataka High Court. The High Court directed the concerned department to pay them equal salary and allowance that are being paid to regular employees. In other case, some persons filed writ petition challenging the order of the State Government directing cancellation of appointments of all casual workers and further direction for regularization of all those workers.

<u>27. The Supreme Court while formulating the law has held that unless the appointments are in terms of the relevant rules and after a proper competition among qualified persons, the same would not confer any right on the appointee. If it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the contract, if it were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end when it is discontinued. Similarly, it was observed, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of appointment. Merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage worker is continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in regular service or made permanent, on the strength of such continuation, if the original appointment was not made by following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules.</u>

<u>28. It has further been observed, it is not open to the Court to prevent regular recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an end or of ad-hoc employees who by the very nature of their appointments do not acquire any right. The High Courts, it is further observed, acting under Article 226 of the Constitution, should not ordinarily issue directions for absorption, regularization, or permanent continuance unless the recruitment itself was made regularly and in terms of the constitutional scheme. The Courts must be careful, it is further observed, in ensuring that they do not interfere unduly with the economic arrangement of its affairs by the State or its instrumentalities or lend themselves the instruments to facilitate the bypassing of the constitutional and statutory mandates. It is also further observed:</u>

<u>"When a person enters a temporary employment or gets engagement as a contractual or casual worker and the engagement is not based on a proper selection as recognized by the relevant rules or procedure, he is aware of the consequences of the appointment being temporary, casual or contractual in nature. Such a person cannot invoke the theory of legitimate expectation for being confirmed in the post when an appointment to the post could be made only by following a proper procedure for selection and in cases concerned, in consultation with the Public Service Commission. Therefore, the theory of legitimate expectation cannot be successfully advanced by temporary, contractual or casual employees. It cannot also be held that the State has held out any promise while engaging these persons either to continue them where they are or to make them permanent. The State cannot constitutionally make such a promise. It is also obvious that the theory cannot be invoked to seek a positive relief of being made permanent in the post."</u>

<u>29. The substance of the opinion is that when statutory rules are framed in exercise of the powers conferred by the Constitution which being exhaustive, the only fair means to adopt is to make appointments basing upon the rules so framed. We do not dispute the statements of law argued above. The Supreme Court in the context of existing laws rightly observed that a temporary employee cannot claim as of right to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of appointment. There is no denial of the fact that merely because a temporary employee or causal worker has been continuing in the service beyond the term of his appointments, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in the regular service merely on the basis of his continuation in service. But in the context of our laws promulgated by the Government for the purpose of absorption in the revenue set up, these cases are to be decided.</u>

<u>30. In the Rules of 2005, the expression ‘উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প’ (development project) defined in section 2 (ka) means, development project approved by the Government during the period between 9th April, 1972 and 30th June, 1997. Naturally, the employees and officers who have been working in respect of those development projects will be eligible for consideration for absorption in the revenue set up, and the other employees and officers either employed on monthly pay scale basis or on daily wage basis in respect of other development projects cannot claim as of right for absorption. In the said rules the expression ‘উন্নয়ন প্রকল্পের কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী’ defined in rule 2 (ga) means, those employees and officers who were appointed on monthly pay scale basis in respect of development project defended in section 2 (ka). So, only those employees and officers will be eligible for consideration who were appointed on monthly pay scale basis in what respect of development projects which were proved during the period mentioned above.</u>

<u>31. For the purpose of regularization certain criteria has been provided in rule 4, such as, (a) if an officer or an employee is appointed in a project following the procedures for appointment rules on the appointment is made in respect of the said project by following the government approved rules; and (b) such officer or employee who has continuity in service; and (c) such officer or employee who has satisfactory service record are eligible for consideration. In Rule 7 the Government reserved power to make such Order in conformity with the rules as far as possible in case of any difficulty for the implementation of the rules. In pursuance of that power ECNEC issued Orders from time to time and the latest one is the memo dated 10th January, 2008 providing that the manpower of a project may be transferred to the revenue budget after completion of the project in which such manpower is working.</u>

32. “স্থানীয় সরকার প্রকৌশল অধিদপ্তর (কর্মকর্তা/কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা,” 2009, (Rules of 2009), provide for the procedure for recruitment in the LGED. It has been provided in Rule 3 that the recruitments shall be made; (Ka) by direct appointment, (Kha) by promotion, (ga) by transfer and (gha) on deputation subject to the conditions prescribed in the schedule and also in order to fulfill the objects provided in Article 29(3) of the Constitution. In the schedule some posts have been reserved for direct recruitment specifying the requisite qualifications. So, the employees and officers of development project cannot claim for being absorbed in those reserved posts. Further, in the said Rules the procedures have been provided to be followed for appointment in those 4 categories of rules 4, 5, 6 and 7. This rules relates to direct recruitment in the LGED but we are concerned with the absorption of the writ petitioners, and there is a specific rules for the said purpose. The absorption rules would hold the field whenever the question of regularization of service would arise.

<u>33. Though do not dispute the ratio in Uma Devi, which are based on recognized principles, in the presence of specific rules for absorption, the opinions expressed in the case will not be applicable in these cases so far as it relates to the officers and employees appointed on monthly pay basis. As observed above, the Rules of 2009 do not debar the regularization of the officers and employees working in the development projects and there is also provision for relaxation of age in respect of certain posts. Besides, the rules of 2005 were promulgated by the President in accordance with Article 140(2) of the Constitution. Therefore, these Rules would govern whenever any vacancy occurs in the revenue budget and the writ respondents ignoring the said rules cannot resort to direct recruitments in respect of certain categories of employees and officers.</u>

34. This Division by judgment dated 14th July, 2011 in Civil Petition Nos. 767, 769, 1084-1085 and 2011 maintained the Judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 5667, 4466 of 2008, 8639, 3218 and 5325 of 2010 on similar facts in respect of some employees and officers working in development projects under LGED. Though it noticed the Rules of 2005 and the decision of the ECNEC dated 31st December, 2007, it did not consider the later decision of ECNEC mentioned above and also did not express any opinion as regards the Rules of 2005 presumably that no argument was made on behalf of the LGED to modify the judgments of the High Court Division in the light of the said Rules and the decision of ECNEC. In fact, when the matters were heard, the LGED did not seriously press for leave and it was made to believe this Division that in view of the absorption of some officers and employees in pursuance of the earlier judgment of the High Court Division, the LGED was left with no option other than to absorb the writ petitioners. Accordingly, this Division did not express any opinion in that regard and affirmed the judgments of the High Court Division mainly on the reasonings that the High Court Division made the rules absolute following the judgment delivered in Writ Petition No. 1522 of 2004 heard along with other 99 writ petitions and there was no reason for not applying the ratio in the said decision. As noticed above, the ratio in the decision given in the above writ petitions are not applicable in these cases, inasmuch as, those cases are quite distinguishable.

35. What is more, in those cases the Rule of 2005 and the ECNEC's decision were not considered. Later on, this Division considered the Rules of 2005 and ECNEC's latest decision in another set of cases and disposed of Civil Petition Nos. 602-603, 649, 673, 679 and 1830 of 2011 by judgment and order dated 5th December, 2001 with the modification of the direction given by this High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 3536, 3559, 3532, 3531, 4456 and 4455 of 2010, as under:

(a) An employee or an officer of any development project can claim for regularization in the revenue set up if the project in which he is working is completed. Such officer or employee must have been appointed after following the (b) recognized procedures being followed by the Government in appointing Government servants.

(c) Such officer or employee must have requisite qualification for the post he is seeking absorption.

(d) Such officer or employee must have continuity in service in the project in which he is working.

(e) Such officer or employee must have satisfactory service record before regularization in the revenue budget.

(f) If an officer and employee whose rank and status did not relate to the posts advertised by the impugned notifications on the day of its publications, such officer or employee will not be eligible for consideration for absorption.

36. When the above petitions were heard, the Rules of 2005 were not placed in extenso and accordingly this Division had considered the Rules superficially and expressed its opinion in the light of the arguments made on behalf of the LGED. This time the learned Attorney-General has placed the different provisions of the rules including definition clauses and tried to satisfy us that all the employees and officers working in the development projects are not entitled to absorption, and the policy of the Government in case of public employment has not been reflected in the judgment which has caused problems in absorbing those officers and workers and thus, these judgments require reconsideration. We have heard the learned Attorney-General and learned Counsel for the writ petitioners at length.

37. On going through the rules and upon hearing the Counsel of both sides, we are satisfied that the earlier judgments require reconsideration. As observed above, the employees and officers of the development projects means those who have been working on monthly pay scale basis in the projects which were approved by the Government during the period between 9th April, 1972 and 30th June, 1997. The employees and officers who were appointed on daily wage basis under master roll scheme do not fall within the definition of employees and officers of development project. They are treated as casual workers employed on contractual basis and thus, their selection was not based on established procedure. However, in the ECNEC's decision it was pointed out that 'সমাপ্ত প্রকল্পের জনবল' to be transferred in the revenue budget, that means, after completion of project all workforce employed in the project would be absorbed. This decision has not singled out the persons employed on daily wage basis. This decision was taken in exercise of powers conferred by rule 7 and therefore, the authority should not keep them outside the ambit of absorption altogether, but at the same time, it should be kept in mind that they do not stand on the same footing with other officers and employees working on monthly pay basis. Therefore, the theory of legitimate expectation or any other theory or principle is not applicable to them. There is another aspect which deserves consideration for their absorption, firstly, that they were not appointed through the backdoor in an irregular manner, and secondly, that the language used in the ECNEC's decision is in wider sense.

<u>38. Most of these employees have been working for a considerable time to the satisfaction of the authority in development projects. There is no doubt that they are experienced workers and contributing towards the development of the country. On consideration of their contribution ECNEC did not exclude them from consideration in the process of absorption. If their services are not accommodated in the revenue budget in vacant posts, they would have to lead miserable lives after the completion of their respective projects. Almost all of them are less qualified persons and because of the age barrier, they would not be able to get any other public employment. It is, therefore, necessary to consider their cases on sympathetic manner and to absorb them against vacant posts by phases according to their seniority. After reviewing all previous judgments and rules, we sum up under;</u>

<u>(i) Whenever any vacancy in LGED is created in the revenue set up, it shall consider for absorption of employees or officers of the development projects within the meaning of section 2(ga) of the Rule, 2005, If the project in which s/he is working is completed 'subject to the condition that such employee or officer has requisite qualifications for the said post.</u>

<u>(ii) Whenever a vacant post is created in the revenue budget, the LGED shall absorb/transfer an employee or officer from the development project mentioned in clause (1) to fill up that post in accordance with Rules of 1985 and the ECNEC's decision dated 10th January, 2008.</u>

<u>(iii) An officer or employee shall be absorbed if s/he was appointed in the development project within the meaning or rule 2(ka) of Rules, 2005 in accordance with the procedures prescribed for appointment in public employment.</u>

<u>(iv) An officer or employee must have requisite qualifications for the post in which he is seeking absorption.</u>

<u>(v) An officer or employee must have continuity in service in the project in which he is working.</u>

<u>(vi) An officer or employee must have satisfactory service record before his case is considered for regularization in the revenue budget.</u>

<u>(vii) If an officer and employee whose rank and status does not relate to the posts advertised by the impugned notifications on the day of its publications, such officer or employee would not be eligible for consideration for absorption.</u>

<u>(viii) The employees and officers who have been working in the development projects mentioned in clause (1) on monthly pay basis would only be eligible for consideration for absorption in the revenue budget.</u>

<u>(ix) Unless and until vacancies in the revenue budget in the LGED are created, the employees and officers of the development project mentioned in clause (1) cannot claim as of right to be absorbed in the revenue budget;</u>

<u>(x) While considering and selecting an employee or officer of the development project for absorption in the revenue budget, the appointing authority shall maintain strictly the prevailing quota system for employment in the public employment being followed by the Government.</u>

<u>(xi) The LGED shall consider the cases of those working on master roll basis for absorption in the revenue budget by phases if they have requisite qualifications subject to availability of vacancies according to their seniority.</u>

The Leave Petitions are disposed of with the above observations and modifications of the earlier as well as the impugned judgments.

End.
